To check Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to report data about people or animals that need an ethics statement, and lacked one.

Show details

The paper appears to analyse data about people, but we could not tell where the data came from. If the authors collected them, or obtained records for this study, an ethics statement is needed. If they come from an open resource such as UK Biobank or NHANES, it is not. We found no ethics statement.

We based this on:

The PMFM strongly correlates with human performance in an existing dataset of melodic predictions.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .432 Indeed, we found that PMFM showed stronger predictive performance for concave melodies (R² = .515, 95% CI [.435, .593]) compared to Temperley (R² = .351, 95% CI [.271, .422]; p <.001), though its performance was statistically comparable to IDyOM (R² = .471, 95% CI [.394, .548]; p = .432).
p = .266 Additionally, the PMFM demonstrated stronger performance for descending melodies (R² = .805, 95% CI [.719, .881]) compared to IDyOM (R² = .671, 95% CI [.581, .755]; p = .012), though it performed comparably to Temperley (R² = .767, 95% CI [.689, .829]; p = .266).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

Duplicated Column Names

  • Duplicated column names in exp2_data.csv. 1 column name appears more than once (worst: file_name×2), so 2 of the file’s 15 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 1 code file.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 474 columns across 24 data files.

Issues Identified

5 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

File Column Issues
HC_data.csv V9 ⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1200 values are missing
HC_data.csv scaleDegree #️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 100% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: “FALSE”
LC_data.csv V9 ⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 1198 values are missing
LC_data.csv scale degree #️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 99% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: “FALSE”
exp2_data.csv file_name 👥 Colliding column names — Column name be…

Cells longer than 300 characters are cut (…).

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 24 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Fine (1)

Fine

Exact P-Values

We found no imprecise p values, p-values of exactly zero or impossible p values out of 25 detected.

Reproducibility Check

We ran the paper’s 1 R script and 2 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script.

1 of 3 scripts ran to the end: 1 did not reproduce, and 1 did not finish within our time limit.

Script Result What happened
analyses.Rmd Ran out of time It was still running after 300 seconds, our time limit per script.
Data_Processing.ipynb Ran to the end
Revision_Analyses.ipynb Stopped with an error AssertionError: AC4

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • analyses.Rmd

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • Revision_Analyses.ipynb

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • analyses.Rmd reads files under another name than the deposit holds (hp_logProbabilities_with_keys.csv -> HP_logProbabilities_with_keys.csv). We corrected the names so the script could run; they should be changed in the script.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 6 statistical tests reported in the paper, 6 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 1 R code file.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 analyses.Rmd — none

File paths

1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: data/hp_logProbabilities_with_keys.csv to data/HP_logProbabilities_with_keys.csv (in analyses.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file.

1 file name in the code is not the same as in the deposit, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

File Name in the code Name in the deposit
analyses.Rmd hp_logProbabilities_with_keys.csv HP_logProbabilities_with_keys.csv

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
analyses.Rmd timed_out timeout 300.4

Calls that install packages in the code

1 call to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Expand a row below to see the output each script produced.

> print_corr_info_boot <- function(responses, model_df, label = "", n_boot = 1000, n_samp = 25) {
>   res <- cor.test(model_df$x, model_df$Y)
>   r <- res$estimate
>   r_squared <- r^2
>   p_val <- res$p.value
>   
>   stem_list <- unique(model_df$item)
>   boot_corrs <- numeric(n_boot)
>   
>   for (i in seq_len(n_boot)) {
>     actual_means <- numeric(length(stem_list))
>     
>     for (j in seq_along(stem_list)) {
>       stem <- stem_list[j]
>       tmp <- responses %>% filter(item == stem)
>       smp <- sample(tmp$MIDI, n_samp, replace = TRUE)
>       actual_means[j] <- mean(smp)
>     }
>     
>     boot_corrs[i] <- cor(actual_means, model_df$Y)
>   }
>   
>   boot_mean <- mean(boot_corrs)
>   ci <- quantile(boot_corrs, c(0.025, 0.975))
>   
>   cat(label, "\n")
>   cat(sprintf("  r = %.3f, R^2 = %.3f, p = %.4f\n", r, r_squared, p_val))
>   cat(sprintf("  Bootstrap mean r = %.3f, 95%% CI [%.3f, %.3f]\n\n", 
>               boot_mean, ci[1], ci[2]))
> }
> full <- df %>%
>   dplyr::select(stem, Human_MIDI, PMFM_round_max) %>%
>   rename(item = stem, x = Human_MIDI, Y = PMFM_round_max)
> ac <- df_hc %>%

> analyze_model_combo <- function(df, predictors, model_names, combo_name) {
>   cat("\n")
>   cat(paste(rep("=", 60), collapse = ""), "\n")
>   cat(sprintf("%-60s\n", paste0(combo_name, " MODEL")))
>   cat(paste(rep("=", 60), collapse = ""), "\n\n")
>   
>   # Build formula
>   formula_str <- paste("Human_MIDI ~", paste(predictors, collapse = " + "))
>   m_full <- lm(as.formula(formula_str), data = df)
>   s_full <- summary(m_full)
>   
>   cat(sprintf("Total R²: %.4f\n", s_full$r.squared))
>   cat(sprintf("Adjusted R²: %.4f\n", s_full$adj.r.squared))
>   cat(sprintf("F-statistic: %.4f, p-value: %.4e\n\n", 
>               s_full$fstatistic[1], 
>               pf(s_full$fstatistic[1], s_full$fstatistic[2], s_full$fstatistic[3], lower.tail = FALSE)))
>   
>   if (length(predictors) > 1) {
>     # Unique variance (ΔR²)
>     cat("---------------- UNIQUE VARIANCE (ΔR²) ----------------\n")
>     delta_R2 <- numeric(length(predictors))
>     names(delta_R2) <- model_names
>     
>     for (i in seq_along(predictors)) {
>       reduced_predictors <- predictors[-i]
>       formula_reduced <- paste("Human_MIDI ~", paste(reduced_predictors, collapse = " + "))
>       m_reduced <- lm(as.formula(formula_reduced), data = df)
>       delta_R2[i] <- s_full$r.squared - summary(m_reduced)$r.squared
>     }
>     
>     print(round(delta_R2, 4))
>     cat("\n% of Total Explained Variance:\n")
>     print(round(100 * delta_R2 / s_full$r.squared, 2))
>     
>     # Partial R²
>     cat("\n---------------- PARTIAL R² (Conditional) ----------------\n")
>     tvals <- s_full$coefficients[-1, "t value"]
>     df_res <- s_full$df[2]
>     partial_R2 <- (tvals^2) / (tvals^2 + df_res)
>     names(partial_R2) <- model_names
>     print(round(partial_R2, 4))
>     
>     # LMG / Shapley
>     cat("\n---------------- LMG / SHAPLEY IMPORTANCE ----------------\n")
>     ri <- calc.relimp(m_full, type = "lmg", rela = TRUE)
>     print(round(ri$lmg, 4))
>     cat("\nProportion of Explained Variance (sums to 1):\n")
>     print(round(ri$lmg / sum(ri$lmg), 4))
>   } else {
>     # Single predictor - just show simple regression stats
>     cat("Single predictor model - no decomposition needed\n")
>     cat(sprintf("Standardized β: %.4f\n", 
>                 s_full$coefficients[2, "Estimate"] * sd(df[[predictors]]) / sd(df$Human_MIDI)))
>   }
>   
>   cat("\n")
>   return(list(model = m_full, summary = s_full))
> }
> cat("\n\n")


> cat(paste(rep("#", 70), collapse = ""), "\n")

> melodies_wide <- read.csv("data/all_melodies_final_means.csv")
> classify_huron <- function(notes) {
>   n <- length(notes)
>   first_pitch <- notes[1]
>   last_pitch  <- notes[n]
>   mid_pitch   <- mean(notes[2:(n - 1)])
> 
>   if (last_pitch > mid_pitch && mid_pitch > first_pitch) {
>     "ascending"
>   } else if (last_pitch < mid_pitch && mid_pitch < first_pitch) {
>     "descending"
>   } else if (first_pitch > mid_pitch && last_pitch > mid_pitch) {
>     "concave"
>   } else if (first_pitch < mid_pitch && last_pitch < mid_pitch) {
>     "convex"
>   } else {
>     "other"
>   }
> }
> huron_contours <- lapply(names(melodies_wide), function(col_name) {
>   vals <- melodies_wide[[col_name]]
>   vals <- vals[!is.na(vals)]
>   notes <- vals[-length(vals)] # drop the trailing human-mean rating
>   data.frame(
>     stemID = trimws(col_name),
>     huron_contour = classify_huron(notes),
>     stringsAsFactors = FALSE
>   )
> }) %>%
>   bind_rows() %>%
>   mutate(huron_shape = case_when(
>     huron_contour %in% c("ascending", "descending") ~ "linear",
>     huron_contour == "convex" ~ "arch",
>     huron_contour == "concave" ~ "u",
>     TRUE ~ "other"
>   ))
> df <- df %>%
>   left_join(
>     huron_contours %>%
>       left_join(melody_names, by = c("stemID" = "original")) %>%
>       select(encoded, huron_contour),
>     by = c("stem" = "encoded")
>   )
> bootstrap_r2_paired <- function(responses, df_sub, predictor_sets, n_boot = 1000, n_samp = 25) {
>   stem_list <- unique(df_sub$stem)
>   model_names <- names(predictor_sets)
>   boot_r2s <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(model_names),
>                      dimnames = list(NULL, model_names))
>   
>   for (i in seq_len(n_boot)) {
>     # Resample ONCE, shared across all models
>     human_means <- sapply(stem_list, function(stem) {
>       tmp <- responses %>% filter(item == stem)
>       mean(sample(tmp$MIDI, n_samp, replace = TRUE))
>     })
>     boot_df <- df_sub %>%
>       mutate(human_mean = human_means[match(stem, stem_list)])
>     
>     for (model_name in model_names) {
>       formula_str <- paste("human_mean ~", paste(predictor_sets[[model_name]], collapse = " + "))
>       fit <- lm(as.formula(formula_str), data = boot_df)
>       boot_r2s[i, model_name] <- summary(fit)$r.squared
>     }
>   }
>   boot_r2s
> }
> subsets <- list(
>   Full   = df,
>   AC     = df_hc,
>   NC     = df_lc
> )
> predictor_sets <- list(
>   PMFM      = "PMFM_round_max",
>   Temperley = "TemperleyHP_key_max",
>   IDyOM     = "IDyOMHP_max"
> )
> boot_matrices <- lapply(names(subsets), function(subset_name) {
>   cat(sprintf("Running: %s\n", subset_name))
>   mat <- bootstrap_r2_paired(all_responses, subsets[[subset_name]], predictor_sets,
>                               n_boot = 1000, n_samp = 25)
>   list(subset = subset_name, mat = mat)
> })
Running: Full
Running: AC
Running: NC
> names(boot_matrices) <- names(subsets)
> results_r2 <- lapply(names(subsets), function(subset_name) {
>   mat <- boot_matrices[[subset_name]]$mat
>   lapply(names(predictor_sets), function(model_name) {
>     vals <- mat[, model_name]
>     data.frame(
>       subset = subset_name,
>       model  = model_name,
>       mean   = mean(vals),
>       lo     = quantile(vals, 0.025),
>       hi     = quantile(vals, 0.975)
>     )
>   }) %>% bind_rows()
> }) %>% bind_rows()
> results_r2$subset <- factor(results_r2$subset, levels = names(subsets))
> results_r2$model  <- factor(results_r2$model,  levels = names(predictor_sets))
> boot_pval_paired <- function(dist_a, dist_b) {
>   diffs <- dist_a - dist_b
>   2 * min(mean(diffs > 0), mean(diffs < 0))
> }
> stars <- function(p) {
>   if (p < 0.001) "***" else if (p < 0.01) "**" else if (p < 0.05) "*" else NA
> }
> get_dist <- function(subset_name, model_name) {
>   boot_matrices[[subset_name]]$mat[, model_name]
> }
> model_offset <- c(PMFM = -0.267, Temperley = 0, IDyOM = 0.267)
> model_pairs  <- list(c("PMFM","Temperley"), c("PMFM","IDyOM"), c("Temperley","IDyOM"))
> y_steps      <- c(0.04, 0.08, 0.12)
> make_annot <- function(subset_names, x_lookup) {
>   rows <- list()
>   for (sn in subset_names) {
>     x_center <- x_lookup[[sn]]
>     max_mean <- max(results_r2$hi[results_r2$subset == sn])
>     for (k in seq_along(model_pairs)) {
>       m1 <- model_pairs[[k]][1]; m2 <- model_pairs[[k]][2]
>       p  <- boot_pval_paired(get_dist(sn, m1), get_dist(sn, m2))
>       s  <- stars(p)
>       if (!is.na(s)) {
>         rows[[length(rows)+1]] <- data.frame(
>           x     = x_center + model_offset[[m1]],
>           xend  = x_center + model_offset[[m2]],
>           y     = max_mean + y_steps[k],
>           label = s
>         )
>       }
>     }
>   }
>   bind_rows(rows)
> }
> cadence_x <- list(AC = 1, NC = 2)
> cadence_annot <- make_annot(c("AC", "NC"), cadence_x)
> add_brackets <- function(p, annot) {
>   if (nrow(annot) == 0) return(p)
>   p +
>     geom_segment(data = annot, inherit.aes = FALSE,
>                  aes(x = x, xend = xend, y = y, yend = y), linewidth = 0.4) +
>     geom_segment(data = annot, inherit.aes = FALSE,
>                  aes(x = x, xend = x, y = y - 0.005, yend = y), linewidth = 0.4) +
>     geom_segment(data = annot, inherit.aes = FALSE,
>                  aes(x = xend, xend = xend, y = y - 0.005, yend = y), linewidth = 0.4) +
>     geom_text(data = annot, inherit.aes = FALSE,
>               aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = y + 0.008, label = label),
>               size = 3.5, family = "sans")
> }
> cadence_plot <- add_brackets(
>   ggplot(results_r2 %>% filter(subset %in% c("AC", "NC")),
>          aes(x = subset, y = mean, fill = model)) +
>     geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
>     geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi),
>                   position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.0) +
>     scale_fill_manual(values = c("PMFM" = "#1f77b4", "Temperley" = "#ff7f0e", "IDyOM" = "#2ca02c")) +
>     labs(x = "Subset", y = expression(R^2), fill = "Model",
>          title = "Bootstrapped R² by Cadence Type") +
>     theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
>     theme(text = element_text(family = "sans"),
>           plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
>           legend.position = "top"),
>   cadence_annot
> )
> ggsave("exports/r2_bootstrap_cadence.png", cadence_plot, width = 6, height = 6, dpi = 300)

> run_shape_combo <- function(df_sub, label) {
>   cat("\n\n")
>   cat(paste(rep("#", 70), collapse = ""), "\n")
>   cat("###", sprintf("%-60s", paste(label, "MODEL COMPARISON ANALYSIS")), "###\n")
>   cat(paste(rep("#", 70), collapse = ""), "\n")
> 
>   # Single-model baselines
>   analyze_model_combo(df_sub, c("TemperleyHP_key_max"), c("Temperley"), "TEMPERLEY ONLY")
>   analyze_model_combo(df_sub, c("IDyOMHP_max"), c("IDyOM"), "IDYOM ONLY")
> 
>   # Two-model combinations
>   analyze_model_combo(df_sub, c("PMFM_round_max", "TemperleyHP_key_max"), c("PMFM", "Temperley"), "PMFM + TEMPERLEY")
>   analyze_model_combo(df_sub, c("PMFM_round_max", "IDyOMHP_max"), c("PMFM", "IDyOM"), "PMFM + IDYOM")
>   analyze_model_combo(df_sub, c("TemperleyHP_key_max", "IDyOMHP_max"), c("Temperley", "IDyOM"), "TEMPERLEY + IDYOM")
> 
>   # Full three-model combination
>   analyze_model_combo(df_sub, c("PMFM_round_max", "TemperleyHP_key_max", "IDyOMHP_max"), c("PMFM", "Temperley", "IDyOM"), "FULL (ALL THREE MODELS)")
> }

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 2 Python code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no source()-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an import loads a module, not the paper’s own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 Data_Processing.ipynb — none
2 Revision_Analyses.ipynb Data_Processing.ipynb dependency

File paths

The data paths in the code to files the repository holds work as deposited, but 1 path names a file the repository does not hold: fragment_ppd_results.csv.

Missing inputs

1 input file the code reads is in the deposit but not usable as named: too large to download, inside an archive, or under a similar name.

File Status Reason
fragment_ppd_results.csv absent referenced file is not present in the repository, but a similarly-named file exists: fragment_ppd_results_multirun.csv

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 1 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt).

All code and output

Reported vs. reproduced

6 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 6 matched (6 fully, 0 partially) — 100% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

Self-reproducible output (JASP / jamovi / SPSS Viewer / Jupyter notebook)

4 JASP/jamovi/SPSS-Viewer/notebook files bundle the analyses and their saved results together, so the reported statistics are recoverable from the files itself, with nothing re-run. We extracted 55 result tables (914 individual statistics), typed with the STATO ontology, and export them as a statistical-output JSON document (in the logs) and as queryable rows.

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We checked 39 references with DOIs. No references with comments in PubPeer were found.

We checked 39 references with DOIs. No citations to articles in the RetractionWatch database were found.
