2.3 Inference

We implemented a particle filtering algorithm to approximate the posterior in Equation 6. Particles are collections of samples that represent possible states of an ongoing melody (i.e., the current note) as well as their associated posterior probability scores. At each time step, the model makes predictions by resampling the current collection of particles (according to their posterior scores) and updating the weights based on newly observed data, assigning higher weights to particles that have a higher likelihood of occurring.

Ultimately, we use these inferences to draw a last note prediction from the generative model, which we compare to human predictions. Particle filtering is well suited to this problem because inference involves jointly tracking uncertainty over musical forces, context across time, and notes.

Inference takes as input sequentially presented notes that together make up a melodic stem (i.e., all notes in a melody except the last note). PMFM's inference procedure does not impose an explicit upper bound on stem length; we evaluate it here on phrase-length sequences consistent with the evaluation corpus and with typical melodic phrase lengths more broadly (e.g., Janssen et al., 2017), and leave extension to longer-range sequences to future work. For each input sequence, we run our particle filter with 1000 particles and at the end of the sequence, return 100 unweighted samples from the posterior for further analysis. For computational convenience, the particle filter is initialized with the ground truth key of the melodic stem as well as the first two notes in the melody. (In future work, this initialization can be carried out using a data-driven proposal for a more accurate process model.) At each following time step, the particle filter state evolves by resampling and updating the weights based on the observed data, which only includes the current note. We implemented this model and our inference procedure in Julia using Gen.jl, a state-of-theart probabilistic programming system (Cusumano-Towner et al., 2019).

Figure 3 shows several runs of the particle filter on four example input melodic stems. We obtain the prediction of a final note (the last time step) by simulating the temporal kernel of the generative model on the unweighted posterior samples (Doucet et al., 2001). From these, we compute the value of the highest-likelihood particle, defined as the particle with the maximum log

2.4 Behavioral Task and Model Simulation

We evaluate our model and compare it to established models of melodic expectation on behavioral data collected by Morgan et al. (2019). This behavioral experiment, which used the melodic expectation paradigm of Fogel et al. (2015), was compared by Morgan et al. to several computa-tional models. This experiment parallels our modeling task in its structure and objective (Figure 1A): it tested melodic expectation in human participants by presenting the opening segments of melodies and asking participants to generate continuations.

2.4.1 Stimuli

The stimuli for this study were melodic stems, short melodic sequences that were truncated to omit the last note. Each melodic stem had two versions: authentic cadence (AC) and non-authentic cadence (NC). These versions differed in the strength of melodic expectation they were designed to elicit (especially to Western listeners). An authentic cadence is a resolution from a dominant chord (harmonic function V), which is subjectively perceived as highly unstable, to another chord, typically the tonic chord (harmonic function I). Non-authentic cadence stems lack such a dominant chord, and thus are not associated with any strong expectation as to what should follow the stem. In other words, AC stems were constructed to end on an implied dominant harmony, which strongly predicts resolution to the tonic (home note); NC stems did not end on a dominant harmony and were designed to avoid creating a strong expectation for any particular continuation.

Crucially, these manipulations of AC and NC were not created with reference to Larson's theory of musical forces. As such, the dataset offers a useful opportunity to evaluate whether our model, which incorporates musical forces, can generalize to melodic contexts that were not explicitly designed around that framework. For analysis, we converted each melodic stem and the corresponding mean of participant responses into MIDI note values, enabling direct comparison with model predictions.

The 45 AC/NC pairs of melodies in this stimulus set were composed by a professional composer (Fogel et al., 2015). They were truncated to form melodic stems ranging from 6-9 notes in length (M = 8.4 notes). The melodies spanned all major keys, contained no non-diatonic pitches, and had mean pitch range of 11.4 semitones (generally within a single octave). Several of these properties directly inform structural choices in the PMFM's generative model: the restriction to 12 (15, with enharmonic spellings) major keys, the use of a single-octave scale per key, and the treatment of "stable notes" as diatonic scale members all reflect corresponding properties of this corpus.

2.4.2 Participants and Procedure

We evaluate the PMFM against previously collected behavioral data rather than new data collected for the present study; full participant and procedural details are reported in the original publications (Fogel et al., 2015; Morgan et al., 2019) and summarized here for completeness. 50 participants were each presented with 45 melodic stems and instructed to sing the note they believed should come next. Each participant heard either the AC or NC version of each stem, yielding behavioral responses for all 90 stimuli across the sample. Participants self-identified as musicians, a characteristic we return to in the Discussion when addressing domain-specific expertise.

2.4.3 Simulation

We simulated our particle filter on each of the 90 melodic stems and obtained a prediction on the final note of each stem, defined as the rounded pitch value corresponding to the highestlikelihood particle -the particle with the maximum log score at the final time step. We compare the predicted note by our model to the average human predictions.

The model includes several free parameters (in total, 11) that control the relative influence of musical forces, the stochasticity of each force component, the rhythm-dependent modulation of forces, the variability in pitch transitions, and measurement noise in pitch observations. The parameters reported here were selected by maximizing the likelihood of the predicted notes under the generative model using a coarse grid search. Appendix Table A1 lists the final parameter values, which are held constant for all subsequent analyses. Full details of the grid search procedure are provided in the Appendix, with Appendix Figs. A1 and A2 showing the log-likelihood of predicted notes for each pair of parameters and correlation to human performance, respectively.

In addition, in Appendix Table A4, we show that the full model achieves a better log-likelihood score relative to its ablations (i.e., removing either of the musical forces or rhythmic regularization). Finally, we emphasize that our results are robust to variation in the model parametersquantitative correlation values vary slightly for nearby shifts in the parameters reported, overall leaving our qualitative results unchanged (Appendix Figs. A3 & A4).

2.5 Transparency and openness

All code and data supporting this study are available at https://osf.io/7sqh6, (Nguyen et al., 2026). Task stimuli, participant responses, and all other study materials were originally created by Morgan et al. (2019) and are available at https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/wgz9t.

3 Results

3.1 PMFM predicts human responses

We examined the linear relationship between the model-predicted notes and human data (Figure 4). We found a strong, positive correlation, r(88) = 0.73, R² = 0.53, p < .001, between the model and humans in predicting a final note for each melody across all stems. A nonparametric bootstrap (1000 resamples) yielded a mean correlation of r = 0.72 with a 95% confidence interval of [0.60, 0.82]. This result suggests that the model's generative structure captures approximately half the variance in people's melodic expectations. r = .73, R² = .53, p < .001

3.2 Similar predictive accuracy for melodic stems of authentic and non-authentic cadence

To further explore model performance, we conducted separate regressions for AC and NC stems.

The model exhibited comparable alignment with human responses across AC stems, r(43) = 0.68 (Bootstrapped 95% CI: [0.48, 0.83], R² = .46, p <.001, and NC stems, r(43) = 0.78 (Bootstrapped 95% CI: [0.61, 0.90], R² = .60, p <.001). This suggests that the PMFM similarly captures melodic expectations in ambiguous or open-ended contexts where tonal resolution is not strongly implied, compared to cases with implied tonal closure. r = .68, R² = .46, p < .001 r = .78, R² = .60, p < .001

3.3 Comparison with established models of melodic expectation

To contextualize the performance of the PMFM, we compared it with two influential computational models of melodic expectation: Temperley's probabilistic model and the IDyOM (Table 1).

Both models were trained on the Pearce-Wiggins corpus, a diverse collection of 903 folk songs and composed melodies (Pearce & Wiggins, 2006). We also tested versions of the IDyOM and Temperley models trained on the larger Essen corpus (Schaffrath & Huron, 1995), a collection of 6,255 folksongs. These results, which we report in Appendix Table A2, are consistent with the Pearce-Wiggins corpus trained models. Like the PMFM, both models were provided as inputs the keys of the melodic stems for which they were predicting human responses. To ensure comparability across models, we extracted the most likely continuation from each model (i.e., the pitch with the highest predicted probability).

3.3.1 Temperley

Temperley's original model is a Bayesian generative framework in which the probability of each possible continuation note is defined by three factors: pitch range (R), which penalizes notes out-side a plausible tessitura (i.e., the range of pitches where most of a melody lies); pitch proximity (P), which favors small differences between consecutive notes; and key (K), which biases toward notes with respect to the corpus-based empirical probability with which each note occurs in a key profile (Temperley, 2008). These components are multiplied to form an "RPK" profile, and their parameter values were estimated from the Pearce-Wiggins corpus described above (Pearce & Wiggins, 2006). Given a melodic prefix and its key, the model outputs a probability distribution across possible continuation notes. Crucially, the model doesn't have structured temporal dynamics like the PMFM, but instead relies on a Brownian process that treats the conditional distribution of the next note as a Gaussian random walk centered on the current note, with standard deviation determined by the RPK profile. We note that Temperley's model is somewhat advantaged a priori as its parameters were tuned on a large corpus of real melodies, whereas our model was not pre-trained on any external dataset.

When combined with the PMFM, the two models together explained 58.1% of variance in human responses (adjusted R² = 0.572, p <.001; Table 1). LMG (Lindeman, Merenda, & Gold; 1980) importance analysis -which fairly attributes shared variance across all possible predictor orderings -indicated that the PMFM and Temperley contributed approximately equally to the combined model (52.8% vs. 47.2%), with PMFM showing slightly greater unique variance (8.8% vs. 5.5%). Notably, the PMFM's contribution is achieved without any pre-training on melodic corpora, highlighting the explanatory power of its force-based representations.

3.3.2 IDyOM

The Information Dynamics of Music (IDyOM) model (Pearce, 2018) is a statistical framework in which melodic expectations arise from probabilistic learning over musical structure. Unlike Temperley's model, which combines a small set of principled constraints, IDyOM estimates conditional probabilities of notes directly from large musical corpora using variable-order Markov models. At each time step, IDyOM assigns probabilities to possible continuations based on long-term (trained on a corpus of Western tonal melodies) and short-term (adapted online to the unfolding melodic context) models. This formulation allows IDyOM to capture both stylistic knowledge learned from the corpus and local phrase-level regularities learned within a single piece. For this analysis, we used a version of the IDyOM trained on the Pearce-Wiggins corpus (Pearce & Wiggins, 2006). To compare IDyOM's predictions with behavioral responses, we selected the output with the highest probability over all possible continuation pitches for each melodic context. We then correlated these predictions with the average human responses.

We find that PMFM and IDyOM perform similarly as single predictors, with PMFM explaining marginally more variance and unique variance than IDyOM (Table 1). The PMFM also explains variance beyond IDyOM. A model including both predictors accounts for 65.0% (adjusted R² = 0.642, p <.001; Table 1) of the variance in human responses, with relative-importance estimates indicating that the PMFM and IDyOM contribute approximately equally to the explained variance (50.2% vs. 49.8%). More notable, however, is that combining the two raises adjusted R² from .518 to .642 -an increase neither model achieves alone, and evidence that force-based priors and corpus-based statistical learning capture complementary, non-redundant structure in human melodic expectation. Like with the Temperley model, the PMFM accounts for unique variance beyond what IDyOM captures, despite not being trained on any musical corpora and despite having far fewer parameters.

3.3.3 Unique variance explained by the PMFM

A regression using all three models collectively explained 65.3% of variance in human melodic expectations (adjusted R² = 0.641, p <.001; Table 1). Unique variance analysis revealed that PMFM contributed 6.9% (p < .001) and IDyOM contributed 7.2% (p < .0001) beyond the other predictors, while Temperley contributed only 0.3%. This pattern was reflected in the regression coefficients, where Temperley's predictor was not statistically significant when controlling for PMFM and IDyOM.

LMG importance indicated more balanced contributions: PMFM (35.8%), IDyOM (35.9%), and Temperley (28.3%). This discrepancy between unique variance and LMG importance reflects existence of shared variance among the models, particularly between Temperley and the other two predictors.

Even in this maximally stringent setting -combining probabilistic constraints (Temperley), corpus-based statistical learning (IDyOM), and force-based representations (PMFM) -the PMFM continued to explain significant unique variance. This demonstrates that force-based representations capture aspects of melodic expectation not reducible to corpus-based statistics models tested here. Even when statistical knowledge about musical style is fully available, force-based representations in the PMFM provide independent predictive leverage, suggesting they reflect cognitive principles distinct from-and complementary to-statistical learning. (It remains possible that a differently trained future statistical model, or a more expressive future version of the PMFM, could absorb from or yield to unique variance each other.)

3.3.4 Differential explanatory power of the PMFM versus other models across melodic contours

To examine whether model performance varied as a function of melodic contour, melodies were categorized into four groups based on Huron's (1996) ascending, descending, convex, and concave (arch-shaped) pitch contours. This categorization allowed us to assess whether the force-based representations implemented in the PMFM confer particular advantages for melodies whose structure is defined by directed contour rather than local tonal patterns (Figure 6).

Of the four types of melodic contours, concave and descending are more predominant in human-composed songs (D. Huron et al., 1996; D. B. Huron, 2006). Concave melodies rise before falling back toward the starting register, while descending melodies move overall downward across the phrase. Both trajectories align naturally with the forces implemented in the PMFM: gravitational pull toward a tonal center creates increasing tension as the melody ascends, while inertia carries the melodic motion forward before gravity reverses the trajectory in the descent. Indeed, we found that PMFM showed stronger predictive performance for concave melodies (R² = .515, 95% CI [.435, .593]) compared to Temperley (R² = .351, 95% CI [.271, .422]; p <.001), though its performance was statistically comparable to IDyOM (R² = .471, 95% CI [.394, .548]; p = .432).

Additionally, the PMFM demonstrated stronger performance for descending melodies (R² = .805, 95% CI [.719, .881]) compared to IDyOM (R² = .671, 95% CI [.581, .755]; p = .012), though it performed comparably to Temperley (R² = .767, 95% CI [.689, .829]; p = .266).

For ascending melodies, where melodies move overall upward over time, all models achieved similar explanatory power (PMFM: R² = .454, 95% CI [.310, .583]; Temperley: R² = .375, 95% CI [.244, .519]; IDyOM: R² = .367, 95% CI [.226, .509]). Only for convex contours, where melodies fall before rising back, did PMFM underperform the corpus-based models (PMFM: R² = .052, 95% CI [.016, .098]; Temperley: R² = .144, 95% CI [.074, .223]; IDyOM: R² = .170, 95% CI [.101, .255]). However, crucially, convex contours were also the most difficult trials for all models -all models we tested showed their weakest correlations to humans on these contours. This result, identified by our fine-grained analysis using Huron's contour types, provides an immediate modeling target for music theorists -a better understanding of melodic expectations in convex contours.

3.3.5 Context-sensitivity of PMFM's predictive distributions across repeated melodic fragments

The above analyses establish that the PMFM produces predictions that align with human expectations and explains variance beyond established statistical models. However, whether PMFM predictions are sensitive to preceding melodic context (as opposed to simply reflecting hyper-local pattern completion) remains unclear. To test this, we investigated cases where short, identical fragments occurred in multiple places with different preceding contexts across the Morgan et al.

(2019) corpus of melodic stems. Restricting to 2-or 3-note fragments with at least one preceding note and one succeeding note (the "ground truth" continuation) yields 878 total fragments.

Further filtering for fragments that occur more than once (range: 2 to 15 occurrences) and whose preceding context differs across occurrences yields 692 such context pairs, drawn from 414 of the 878 candidate fragments.

For each of the 414 fragments, we obtained a posterior predictive distribution over the note immediately following the fragment by conditioning the PMFM's particle filter jointly on the preceding context and the fragment, rather than on the complete stem. We compared these predic-tions to those of the IDyOM, which assigns a predictive distribution at every note position within a melody (unlike the Temperley model, which assigns probability globally rather than at each time step). We calculated the Jensen-Shannon and symmetrized Kullback-Leibler divergence between the model's full predictive distributions (each represented as a discrete distribution over integer pitch, rounding the PMFM's particles to the nearest semitone to match IDyOM's representation), and correlated this divergence with the absolute difference in ground-truth continuations. Because pairs sharing a fragment are not statistically independent, significance was assessed via a cluster bootstrap resampling whole fragments (1,000 resamples).

PMFM's distributional divergence reliably tracked the magnitude of the true context effect (KL and JS divergence both r ≈ .26-.27, p < .001), whereas IDyOM's did not (r ≈ .02-.04, both ns; Table 2). This pattern is consistent with the PMFM's predictive distribution responding to preceding melodic context in a way that is not captured by IDyOM, at least for the available fragments in the current corpus, providing further evidence for the PMFM's musical-forces-based representations.

4 Discussion

We presented the Probabilistic Musical Forces Model, a model of human melodic expectations that synthesizes components from computational modeling and music-theoretic accounts of this process that so far remained separate: Temperley's probabilistic inference of structure from surface A key distinction of our model, relative to both Temperley's model and IDyOM, is that the PMFM does not rely on prior exposure to a large musical corpus. Our model captures a form of melodic reasoning that may be structurally grounded rather than statistically learned. At the same time, our framework, which includes probabilistic formulation and approximate Bayesian inference, is not opposed to statistical learning and can facilitate further extensions. Such statistical learning can inform the PMFM's prior over keys (Temperley, 2008), yield a mixture distribution over transitions based on a combination of forces and statistics, and support more efficient inference (Dasgupta et al., 2020), including data-driven proposals for inferring key and initial note in a sequence. This extensibility also points to a current limitation of the PMFM's constructs. The model does not itself explain how forces like gravity, magnetism, and inertia are acquired, nor does it account for variations in expertise or cultural variation in melodic expectation -questions statistical learning accounts are naturally suited to address, and which integrating the two approaches may help resolve.

Still, the PMFM's contribution persists even when evaluated alongside established statistical models. In each pairwise comparison, PMFM, Temperley, and IDyOM all explained statistically significant unique variance in human responses (Table 1), indicating that none of the three fully subsumes the others. This demonstrates that the force-based representations formalized in the PMFM capture aspects of melodic expectation not reducible to corpus-based statistics alone. In other words, even when statistical knowledge about musical style is fully available, force-based dynamics provide independent predictive leverage, suggesting that they reflect cognitive principles distinct from -and complementary to -statistical learning. More directly, linear combinations of the PMFM and statistical models, especially the IDyOM model, yield significantly higher correlations with behavior than either model alone, further indicating the appeal of integrating these two approaches.

The PMFM's force-based representations provide additional insight into human musical cognition beyond explained variance. First, the predominance of descending and concave (archshaped) melodic contours in human songs has been attributed to motoric energy efficiency and is thought to be shared with non-human songs, specifically bird songs (Tierney et al., 2011). The (Abrams et al., 2022; Boso et al., 2006; Gold et al., 2019).

To perform these further empirical evaluations effectively, future work should address limitations of the current implementation of PMFM. First, the PMFM (like IDyOM and Temperley's model) is currently provided the ground-truth key of each melodic stem; instead, it should infer it as part of its posterior. Although the PMFM readily induces uncertainty over final notes via its particle representation, the spread of this distribution does not significantly increase for NC stems in the way that human response variability does (albeit numerically, it is in the right direction; see Appendix Figure A5); representing this and other sources of uncertainty due to key might help PMFM capture additional contextual uncertainty that drives ambiguous melodic expectations.

Second, the PMFM's key representation, scale structure, and evaluation are all specific to Western tonal music in major keys, and the model makes no claims about melodic expectation in other musical systems. Many musical traditions organize pitch, scale, and stability differently than the diatonic, equal-tempered framework assumed here -including non-Western tonal systems, microtonal and non-equal-tempered scales, and modal or non-tonal organizational principles. Even within Western tonal music, harmonic context substantially shapes melodic perception and expectation. Extending the model's forces to incorporate harmonic context and a richer diversity of tonal and musical systems is an exciting direction for future work, as is exploring richer force-like relational structures -e.g., from the intuitive physics of non-rigid solids and fluids (Bates et al., 2019; Bi et al., 2025), other domains of musical cognition (Fram & Berger, 2023), and more generally the structured representations in cognitive science writ large (Sablé-Meyer et al., 2022) -beyond those considered by Larson and formalized by PMFM, that might map these traditions. Third, music involves temporally elongated, event-like structures, much like intuitive physics (e.g., a collision event, the dynamics pattern of a bouncing ball, (Yates et al., 2024)). While our current model incorporates basic rhythm through latent metrical positions that modulate force strength, future versions should account for richer temporal structures underlying melodies, including hierarchical meter and even qualitative aspects such as emotion and articulation (Fitzroy & Sanders, 2015; Sun et al., 2020; Trost et al., 2015). Such extensions could be realized by incorporating "invisible surface" (as in Little and Firestone, 2021) into PMFM's generative model, which could flexibly introduce force relations to its temporal kernel. Such invisible surfaces would also afford some degree of algorithmic surprise that may align with listener intuitions in more open-ended melodies.

Our findings demonstrate that force-based representations capture substantial variance in human expectations that extends beyond corpus-based statistical models. Future extensions of the PMFM should incorporate mechanisms for learning tonal structure and richer hierarchical temporal representations, and should test it against diverse musical styles and listening populations. By grounding melodic prediction in a constrained, interpretable framework, we hope this work contributes to a deeper understanding of how humans anticipate and make sense of melodic structure in music.

Constraints on generality

The participants in the melodic continuation study (originally conducted by Morgan et al., 2019) were self-identified musicians, which raises the possibility that their responses reflect domainspecific training rather than purely intuitive expectations. However, the close alignment between the PMFM's predictions and those of the participants -despite the model being untrained on stylistic or performance data -suggests that human performance in our behavioral dataset reflects more general cognitive constraints underlying melodic prediction rather than merely mirroring learned musical conventions. Additionally, the composed melodies and trained models in this study represent Western musical conventions. Future work should further evaluate the PMFM by examining predictions across listeners with differing musical backgrounds. Also see Discussion.

Model Predicted Note LL Full -2.96 ± 0.06 No Gravity -3.00 ± 0.05 No Magnetism -3.00 ± 0.06 No Inertia -2.99 ± 0.07 where p(K) is a uniform prior over keys and p(Note 1 | K) is a normal distribution centered around the corresponding key's home note, and p(Note 2 | Note 1 , K) initializes the second note as a normal distribution centered on the first observed note, p(Note2 | Note 1 , K) = N (Note 1 , σ note ) (requiredto establish the initial direction of melodic motion for the inertia force, which acts on the interval between the two preceding notes).

For t ≥ 3, the one-step transition term p(Note t , F t-1 , ∆t t-1 | Note t-1 , Note t-2 , K) factorizes into a prior over rhythmic advances p(∆t t-1 ), a force distribution p(F t-1 | Note t-1 , Note t-2 , K), which is the weighted linear combination of the three individual force distributions -gravity, magnetism, and inertia -each modeled as a normal distribution whose mean is computed from the preceding notes and key (as defined in Section 2.2.2), and a rhythm-modulated pitch transition p(Note t | Note t-1 , F t-1 , ∆t t-1 ) that generates the next latent note (Eq. 5). Finally, p(x t | Note t ) captures the likelihood function linking latent notes to surface observations.This posterior -the model's updated probability distribution over the melody's hidden structure, given the notes observed so far -in Eq. 6 formalizes melodic expectation as sequential probabilistic inference in a structured generative model, combining a key-based representation of global tonal structure with context-sensitive force components and latent temporal transitions, inspired by the theories of Larson and Temperley. In the following, we provide the details of this generative model and our particle filtering inference procedure for approximate posterior inference.

and

Larson's theory of musical forces as the drivers of melodic expectations. Our model integrates these perspectives within a generative framework that unfolds melodies based on an underlying key structure and the algorithmic influence of musical forces such as gravity, magnetism, and inertia. The model also incorporates rhythm as a fundamental component, with latent rhythmic transitions modulating both the magnitude and uncertainty of musical forces. Inference under this model yields predictive distributions that correlate with average human melodic expectations, providing support for our intuitive-physics-based approach.

PMFM's especially strong consistency with human performance on these two melodic shapes suggests it captures core intuitive expectations of musical cognition with roots beyond domainspecific training. Second, our analysis of context-sensitivity across repeated melodic fragments offers support for the PMFM's force-based representations: only the the PMFM's predictive distributions reliably tracked the magnitude of true context effects in how a fragment's preceding material shaped its continuation. It is possible that a future statistical model trained on a much larger corpus will also show similar context-sensitivity, which further indicates the appeal of the PMFM as a cognitively plausible account: without training and performing domain-general inference mechanisms (i.e., Bayesian inference) over a structured generative model already yields predictions sensitive to melodic context in a way not reducible to local pattern completion. Future work should evaluate these insights in datasets beyond what we studied here, including testing them on predictions by listeners with differing musical backgrounds, and especially children, whose limited musical experience may provide a clearer window into early-developing aspects of melodic expectation. More broadly, future work should evaluate the PMFM and alternatives on a broader range of measures of melodic expectation, including surprisal, uncertainty, and neurological responses, across more varied musical contexts
